item.title: Transcending the trust boundaries: how a cloud pentest works
item.description:
Authors

  • Matvey Bukhtoyarov
  • Denis Stepanov
  • Kaspersky Security Services

Users trust a cloud provider to configure and maintain their IT services, including data storage. In turn, the provider guarantees that hosted services will stay up and that data will remain strictly confidential.

To demonstrate that their platforms are secure, providers choose different strategies: some run bug bounty programs, some rely on regular internal audits, and some bring in external research teams. However, cloud pentest methodology still has plenty of blind spots: there’s no single standard, and the outcome depends on the experience and skill of the team.

Most pentests in this area have historically focused on the external layer: the management console, customer interfaces, APIs, and the basic network perimeter. This layer is important, but it’s only the surface.

In this introductory article, we share our approach to penetration testing of cloud environments, which we’ve developed over several years and dozens of projects. We don’t claim to cover every possible scenario. Instead, we want to show the reasoning behind our pentests and highlight less obvious points that are easy to miss.

Key points

  • Cloud infrastructure is more complex than a traditional web application. To simplify, you can think of it as a hotel with three zones: the booking website (External, the outermost layer), the guest rooms (Overlay, the logical layer), and the staff area (Underlay, the infrastructure or base layer). A cloud service is well protected if the trust boundaries between these zones cannot be breached.
  • A cloud pentest’s value isn’t measured by the number of vulnerabilities found or by the mere fact that code ran. Remote command execution in an isolated tenant container is only the beginning of a pentest, not the end. The main goal is to assess whether an attacker can violate trust boundaries.
  • The assessment should answer five critical questions: Can an attacker read, modify, or delete other tenants’ data? Can they take over the provider’s IAM service account? Does compromising a runtime environment lead to the attack spreading to other resources and services? Can the provider’s internal resources be affected from low-trust segments? Is a virtual environment escape possible?
  • A negative result is still a result. If a pentester cannot move from the tenant plane to the provider overlay, that is a valuable finding. It shows which protection boundaries work in practice and which rely only on assumptions and need additional controls. However, it does not prove that the trust boundary is impossible to cross or that no other attack paths exist.

Key terms

Below, we explain some specific terms that are most often used in cloud infrastructures.

Show definitions

Tenant (think of a renter in an apartment building) is a logically isolated unit within a cloud platform. Examples include a user (such as an organization), a separate project or cloud account, or another unit of administrative and resource isolation.

Tenant plane is the set of IT services and data that a tenant manages directly: virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, databases, object storage, and managed applications.

Management console is the graphical web interface and the entry point for the customer at the External layer.

Service runtime is the actual environment in which a provider’s cloud product runs: a process, container, pod, virtual machine, or microVM.

Service management plane consists of the provider’s internal components that create, update, restart, back up, and delete the service runtime.

IAM service account (service identity) is a special digital identity for programs, bots, cloud services, or servers. It lets them access the required cloud resources automatically and securely, without human involvement.

Context (in cloud security) is the set of attributes and credentials that define the current permissions and runtime environment of a subject in the system. It includes the identity in use (for example, a service account token, certificate, or key), the privilege level (roles and IAM policies), and the technical environment from which the request is initiated (container, virtual machine, or network segment).

Initial zone is the context in which the researcher lands right after the first successful transition. It consists of the specific runtime, IAM service account (service identity), namespace, network routes, and the set of available services.

Provider overlay is the provider’s internal environment, hidden from the customer, that is accessible from the initial zone: network segments, DNS zones, internal APIs, and management components.

Control plane consists of the platform components that make global management decisions and change the platform state: they allocate resources, assign permissions, configure the network, and coordinate state.

Data plane consists of the components that transfer or process user data and application traffic. Some components (or systems) sit at the intersection of different architectural layers, so they can’t automatically be assigned to the data plane or the control plane. Examples include logging, backup and billing systems. Their role changes depending on the task a component is performing at a given moment and how its work affects user traffic.

Cell is a bounded portion of the platform in which compute, disk, network, or management components are shared (often tied to a region, availability zone, service type, or group of tenants).

Pods are the smallest compute units in Kubernetes. A pod is one or more containers that are deployed on the same host and share common resources.

Cross-tenant impact is confirmed impact from the context of one tenant on the resources of another, without a trust relationship defined by the architecture.

Provider-level impact is impact on a provider’s management, infrastructure, or supply chain component that goes beyond the original tenant resource.

Tenant workload is the set of compute resources, processes, and applications that a customer runs and uses in their tenant to perform business tasks. It includes virtual machines, containers (such as pods in Kubernetes), serverless functions, managed databases, and any other active services that process tenant data.

What a pentester needs to check

During a project, a pentester needs to examine not only the management console but also the boundaries that separate the tenant plane from managed services and the provider’s internal infrastructure. A single request passes through many components, from the API gateway to the storage system. A configuration error in any of them changes the attack context: the researcher takes over an IAM service account, gains access to the cloud’s internal network, or acquires the ability to affect another tenant.

This is why a cloud pentest is not just a search for vulnerabilities in the management console, nor a sequential scan of cloud subnets. Above all, it means testing trust boundaries: verifying how transitions between zones with different trust levels are controlled. A more trusted zone must treat everything that comes from a less trusted zone as potentially hostile.

What makes a boundary real? Controls such as authentication and authorization (IAM, RBAC), isolation (virtualization, containerization, network segmentation), cryptography (mTLS), input handling, and others. We build a map of potential boundaries and check each one: is it actually enforced by controls, or does it rely on assumptions (architectural, infrastructural, implementation-related, and others)?

Cloud platform as a research target

When we assess the security of a traditional system, we usually start from basic architectural patterns. For web applications, this is a typical stack of a web server (Nginx, Apache, and so on), server-side logic, object storage, and integrations with third-party services. For hardware solutions, it is a chain from physical interfaces to firmware and protocol handlers.

Cloud platforms are different: how they’re actually built is highly uncertain. Cloud computing standards and reference architectures (such as NIST SP 800-145 and ISO/IEC 17788) define the roles of participants and the relationships between cloud components, but they don’t prescribe strict rules for how to build a platform.

Because there is no single technical standard, a managed database that looks the same from the outside can run in an isolated virtual machine at one provider, in a namespace of a shared Kubernetes cluster at another, and in a dedicated tenant cluster at a third. The same variability applies to software choices. A provider can use OpenStack, Kubernetes, its own control plane, or a combination of them. This means a familiar product name doesn’t give a full picture of the system’s internal structure.

That’s why a cloud pentest is harder than assessing a traditional system. Once the tenant trust boundary is breached (say, by escaping from a microVM to the host operating system), the job is no longer finding the next open port. It becomes reconstructing the architecture from indirect clues. The pentester puts the puzzle together by studying running processes, network routes, certificates, service names, and agent configurations. From these details, the researcher determines the role of each component and the trust boundaries between them.

To keep our approach vendor-agnostic, we will look at cloud infrastructure without reference to specific brands. Depending on the architectural scenario, the same component can be implemented in fundamentally different ways. For example, in one case a managed database can run as a separate managed service isolated at the virtual machine level (where the main risks are hypervisor security and the management API). In another case, it can run as a container inside a shared Kubernetes cluster (where the threat comes from the possibility of container-to-host escape and the quality of namespace isolation).

The hotel analogy and the three cloud layers

There is no single standard for building cloud infrastructure. To make pentesting systematic, we use our own three-layer model of the cloud: External, Overlay, and Underlay. The easiest way to picture a cloud platform is as a large hotel. It has a public area for guests, back-of-house areas for staff, and technical floors with utility systems. This analogy doesn’t cover every detail, but it shows well how areas of responsibility are divided and how the transitions between them work.

External layer: in a hotel, this is the booking website, the doors, and the front desk. At this layer, the pentester interacts with cloud components the way a typical user does: logs in to an account, calls the public API, creates IT services, and connects to their endpoints. Work at this layer is similar to external penetration testing or application security assessment. The main goal is to gain initial access from the outside to another customer’s tenant, or to move to the Overlay layer.

The External layer is where tenant access is provided as intended. In a hotel, the tenant is the room itself: guests control the belongings and equipment in their own room, but their key card must not open neighboring rooms. In the cloud, customers manage only their own data, virtual machines, pods, databases, object storage (S3 buckets), and accounts within their own project. A tenant is not a separate infrastructure layer. It is what the user gets at the External layer. This is where the user’s legitimate privileges end and the first trust boundary, the one the pentester checks, begins.

The provider’s service layer (Overlay): in a hotel, this is the “Staff only” area: kitchens, laundries, the control room, service corridors, and the master key system. In cloud infrastructure, this is the internal logical service management layer: runtime environments for managed services, schedulers, backup, monitoring (observability) and billing systems, the IAM system, and internal APIs. Customers use the results provided by these systems but must not get any access to them unwarranted by the architecture.

Don’t confuse this term with an overlay network in traditional network engineering: a logical network on top of a transport underlay network, such as VXLAN segments. In our methodology, Overlay has a broader meaning: it’s the internal logical layer for running and managing cloud services, and it can be split differently depending on the cloud. For clarity, the table below divides it into two sublayers: runtime environments of tenant services and provider’s internal components.

Infrastructure layer (Underlay): in a hotel, this is the utilities, electrical equipment, and physical access control systems that keep the building running. In the cloud, this is the hardware layer: physical servers, host operating systems, hypervisors, the transport network, storage systems, and out-of-band management. Careless testing at this layer can do serious damage.

But the key point of this analogy is not the rooms themselves, but the doors between them. A vulnerability on a booking website is dangerous, but a master key left in a room that opens several or every door in the building is far more so. The same rule applies in the cloud: remote code execution (RCE) inside an isolated tenant container (pod) is only a local problem. Only after that does it finally reach the infrastructure layer.

Each transition changes the trust zone, but it doesn’t necessarily mean reaching a new subnet or obtaining root privileges. It’s like passing through turnstiles inside the same building. We haven’t left the building (a new subnet) or gotten keys to every door (root privileges), but at each checkpoint we have our badge checked again, because different security rules apply on the other side. At the boundary between an API and a worker, a vulnerability can arise from differences in data handling. For example, an internal cloud API accepts a string containing a null byte (\x00) from a user, considers it valid, and passes it on. A background worker then blindly trusts this data and inserts it into a low-level query to a PostgreSQL database. In C libraries, \x00 terminates a string. As a result, the database handler truncates the text at the point where this byte was injected. This breaks the logic of the SQL query or permission check and resets the regular user’s context. The system is then forced to change the password of the main administrator (postgres), which leads to full database takeover.

A customer rents a managed database in their tenant. The tenant is allowed to run SQL queries but not allowed to connect to the operating system the database runs on. Here, the trust boundary lies between the permissions of a database role and the runtime environment of the database process. If, through the permitted SQL queries, the pentester manages to reach code execution at the operating system level as the service process, the pentester gains full access to the host’s resources. This lets them do more than just collect information. They can actively interact with the host: read and modify files, analyze running processes, establish network connections to internal services, and extract credentials (for example, an IAM service account token) to attack other cloud components.

Example 2. Legitimate access (managed virtual machine)

In another implementation, the provider supports SSH key authentication by design, and the user connects to the resource like to any other virtual machine. Formally, the product is still called a “managed database”, but the actual trust boundary shifts deeper, to the level where the guest OS interacts with the host infrastructure. In this case, SSH access to the operating system is not a violation in itself, because the service model allows it. What we need to test is the next boundary, the one between the service virtual machine and the management agents, metadata, host, or control plane.

This leads to several practical rules:

  • Normal execution of user code does not, by itself, prove an isolation breach. In IT services such as interactive notebooks, continuous integration (CI) runners, or serverless systems, code execution is a product feature.

  3. The target object grants specific permissions to the current context. This is not yet the execution of dangerous operations, but only a check that they are allowed.
  4. Controlled action beyond the original trust boundary. The researcher performs the minimum safe action that confirms the previously obtained permissions work in practice. For example, they create a test record in a neighboring tenant (usually a second test tenant).

  1. External attacker without an account. The test covers the public attack surface, registration, the login mechanism, externally accessible services, and the path to the first tenant context. Layer: External.
  2. Attacker with legitimate tenant access. This is the key model for a multi-tenant cloud: the tenant is entitled to create their own resources and tries to go beyond the limits those resources impose. Layer: External.

The pentester interacts with the managed service interface and finds a vulnerability in it (for example, CVE-2026-19478 in the case of the GitLab web interface) or in add-on modules deployed by the cloud provider. The chain begins with the compromise of a tenant workload. The researcher plants malicious code in a popular OS or container image in advance. A cloud tenant downloads and runs the trojanized image, and the attacker gains access inside that specific container. Next, the attacker finds ways to escape the container (using CVE-2026-43284) into the runtime: the container runtime, hypervisor, or host agent. From there, they reach the host shared with other containers and can affect the provider’s management components.

2. Credentials first

Rather than gaining access to a runtime environment, the researcher may obtain credentials that cloud services accept as valid: a service account token, metadata access credentials, an mTLS certificate, a bootstrap token, or an object storage key.

In this scenario, the move into the provider overlay doesn’t come from breaking network isolation. It happens through legitimate platform functionality. The network may be well segmented, but an over-privileged IAM service account token that the attacker manages to extract (for example, from environment variables or metadata) can legitimately call an internal API through a standard gateway or token exchange service.

3. Administrative or service context

The goal of this scenario is to bypass technical restrictions by gaining legitimate access through channels intended for staff. The route often starts with targeting people (phishing, insiders, or leaked employee or contractor credentials). However, the final entry point into the internal environment is technical: a connection through the operator’s VPN, a support portal, a remote support tool, an administrative workstation, an SSH certificate, or a serial console. Although the route often starts with compromising a person, the resulting initial zone (the technical context with certain privileges and access to resources where the researcher ends up) can match the first scenario. For example, access to a managed database host (DBaaS host) can be obtained not by exploiting a vulnerability but through a legitimate administrative channel, which is then used for privilege escalation.

After moving deeper into the cloud infrastructure and gaining access to a node, the pentester analyzes local artifacts. Completely different architectures can hide behind the same managed service.

OpenStack-like infrastructure

IaaS services based on OpenStack usually include a large set of components: an IAM service account, compute resources, networking, images and block storage, as well as API processes, workers, a message broker, and platform state databases. A managed service built on top of such an IaaS layer can use a separate virtual machine for each database instance, several instances on a shared virtual machine, a Kubernetes cluster on virtual workers, or even a dedicated tenant for a specific product.

A message broker such as RabbitMQ is typical for OpenStack, but finding one doesn’t prove that the target is a stock OpenStack deployment. The provider may have changed the trust model, added its own API, and replaced some of the components.

Kubernetes-based platforms

In clouds of this type, a central Kubernetes cluster controls the entire infrastructure: not only containers but also virtual machines, other tenant Kubernetes clusters, and managed services. At the service runtime level, a product can run as a pod in a shared namespace, an application inside a tenant, a KubeVirt virtual machine, or a worker node of a separate cluster. From the outside, they all look like the same product, but their trust boundaries and the attack surface behind them differ radically.

Because the platform is managed through a Kubernetes cluster, where the service account token is the main unit of authorization, it’s especially important to determine where the IAM service account you obtained during the pentest lives: in a tenant cluster, in a managed cluster, or with an operator that serves multiple tenants. Identical-looking tokens may have permissions for only one pod, or they may allow changing resources in several environments at once.

Custom control plane and configuration management systems

A provider may forgo off-the-shelf platforms altogether. For example, in this kind of architecture, a provider might build its public API in-house, deploy virtual machines through libvirt or a lightweight IaaS layer, automate networking with scripts around Open vSwitch (OVS), build object storage on Ceph, and distribute node configuration through SaltStack or another configuration management system.

In this architecture, a virtual machine management service might get its settings from an internal HTTP service, a script with shared credentials might run backups, billing might receive events from a queue, and an internal agent might talk to the control plane over mTLS. Almost every component here is specific to the provider. The main risk area is not vulnerabilities in well-known products, such as those built on open-source solutions, but logic errors at the junctions between internal systems.

Mixed-stack platform

In practice, the most common setup is a mix of approaches

  1. The infrastructure core (IaaS layer) is built on OpenStack
  2. Kubernetes runs the managed services
  3. The storage system runs on Ceph
  4. IAM, billing systems, and the internal API are custom-built.

Here are some clues that can help form initial hypotheses about the environment:

  • A Kubernetes token and cluster DNS in the runtime environment of the host under investigation suggest that the service is running in the context of a pod.
  • A running qemu-guest-agent process indicates that we are inside a virtual machine rather than on a physical server.
  • Attached Ceph/RBD volumes point to a separate storage plane in the platform architecture, implemented as distributed block storage.
  • A large number of CNI or Open vSwitch (OVS) network interfaces means that this is a shared Kubernetes node

However, any such clue needs additional verification tests.

Example of a mixed-stack cloud platform

How to choose the next trust boundary

After the pentester has examined the initial zone, the next route depends on a combination of two factors:

  1. Network visibility: which segments, services, and tenants are reachable.
  2. Available trust level: which credentials, certificates, and API methods are accepted as valid in those segments.

Sometimes the network has almost no restrictions, but all services require correct mTLS authentication. In other cases, the network is almost completely closed, but a discovered service account can create resources across the entire region through the standard API. For this reason, network reachability (open ports) and the IAM service account must be considered together.

At this stage, the researcher usually focuses on several critical areas:

Telemetry (observability): the pentester checks whether centralized monitoring systems (logs, metrics, traces) collect data from different tenants and whether there is sufficient isolation between them. Isolation can fail if an attacker can search by other tenants’ identifiers, read raw event records, extract credentials from telemetry events, or influence alerts and automated actions.

Overlay (IT services) Service runtime: the operating system and its components, provider and product agents, and database engine. User SQL queries, code executed inside jobs, imported plug-ins, or operating system images. Break out of the service runtime, find excessive privileges on the IAM service account (service identity) assigned to it.
Overlay (provider components) Billing system, backups, monitoring, access control system, and internal cloud API. A confirmed initial zone obtained at the previous step or provided by the cloud provider to save time. Breach the boundaries between services, disrupt tenant isolation, find ways to interact with the control plane or IT services.
Underlay Host operating systems, virtualization systems (hypervisors), the transport network, storage systems, baseboard management controllers (BMC), and other low-level mechanisms. A virtual machine the pentester controls, with access to the underlay, or a privileged IAM service account (service identity). Check the isolation of virtualization and neighboring workloads, as well as the real scale of the impact.

A real cloud platform doesn’t always fit this matrix. A service can run in a separate virtual machine, in a pod in a shared cluster, or in a microVM. A hypervisor belongs to the Underlay, but its management API may be reachable from the Overlay. That’s why the layer a pentester is currently on (External, Overlay, or Underlay) depends not just on the IP address but on four attributes taken together:

  1. Who controls the cloud infrastructure component.
  2. Whose data and resources the component serves.
  3. Which IAM service account is used for interaction.
  4. How far its privileges extend.

Where the trust boundaries lie

When analyzing the network that supports a cloud’s internal infrastructure, it’s easy to wrongly assume there is only one trust boundary, between the tenant and the provider. But reaching the provider’s internal network may be only the first step. A real platform contains many zones with different trust levels, and compromising one component doesn’t necessarily give access to the whole infrastructure. For example, a user request may pass in sequence through the customer interface (the management console), then the tenant plane (a database), then the service runtime (the virtual machine that the database runs on), then the service management plane (an internal service that monitors database health), then the cloud control plane (an internal service that manages database resources). Only after that does it finally reach the infrastructure layer.

Each transition changes the trust zone, but it doesn’t necessarily mean reaching a new subnet or obtaining root privileges. It’s like passing through turnstiles inside the same building. We haven’t left the building (a new subnet) or gotten keys to every door (root privileges), but at each checkpoint we have our badge checked again, because different security rules apply on the other side. Sometimes the boundary lies between two roles in the same process, sometimes between an API and a worker, and sometimes between a guest virtual machine and a hypervisor. At the boundary between an API and a worker, a vulnerability can arise from differences in data handling. For example, an internal cloud API accepts a string containing a null byte (\x00) from a user, considers it valid, and passes it on. A background worker then blindly trusts this data and inserts it into a low-level query to a PostgreSQL database. In C libraries, \x00 terminates a string. As a result, the database handler truncates the text at the point where this byte was injected. This breaks the logic of the SQL query or permission check and resets the regular user’s context. The system is then forced to change the password of the main administrator (postgres), which leads to full database takeover.

Example 1. Strict isolation (managed database)

A customer rents a managed database in their tenant. The tenant is allowed to run SQL queries but not allowed to connect to the operating system the database runs on. Here, the trust boundary lies between the permissions of a database role and the runtime environment of the database process. If, through the permitted SQL queries, the pentester manages to reach code execution at the operating system level as the service process, the pentester gains full access to the host’s resources. This lets them do more than just collect information. They can actively interact with the host: read and modify files, analyze running processes, establish network connections to internal services, and extract credentials (for example, an IAM service account token) to attack other cloud components.

Example 2. Legitimate access (managed virtual machine)

In another implementation, the provider supports SSH key authentication by design, and the user connects to the resource like to any other virtual machine. Formally, the product is still called a “managed database”, but the actual trust boundary shifts deeper, to the level where the guest OS interacts with the host infrastructure. In this case, SSH access to the operating system is not a violation in itself, because the service model allows it. What we need to test is the next boundary, the one between the service virtual machine and the management agents, metadata, host, or control plane.

This leads to several practical rules:

  • Normal execution of user code does not, by itself, prove an isolation breach. In IT services such as interactive notebooks, continuous integration (CI) runners, or serverless systems, code execution is a product feature.
  • Gaining maximum privileges inside a pod does not mean gaining maximum privileges on the node. After crossing each trust boundary (for example, into a zone with different privileges or service accounts), you need to re-check what’s visible: processes, mount points, interfaces, devices, and IAM service accounts.
  • An IAM service account token that a researcher finds is not necessarily useful. What matters is who issued it and which systems accept it. The tenant or service the token is bound to, and the actions it permits there, also matter.
  • The fact that a tenant container can reach a provider’s internal IP address does not mean a compromise has occurred. In many clouds, some internal services are reachable over the network by design. For a real compromise, an attacker must either steal a service token or find an internal service that mistakenly accepts customer accounts or requires no authentication.
  • Remote code execution inside the environment where a service runs does not mean access to the control plane. This is only the initial zone, from which the researcher must look for the next trust boundary: service tokens, the provider’s internal APIs, and neighboring containers.

To tell a real trust boundary violation from a false positive, we use four sequential stages from the researcher’s perspective:

  1. Network visibility. The researcher can see the provider’s internal service from the tenant plane. This is not a breach yet, but it is the first sign that isolation may be insufficient.
  2. The researcher manages to authenticate to a service by presenting a token or certificate compromised at the previous step (for example, a service account token or a metadata token). This is serious, because the service treats the request as legitimate.
  3. The target object grants specific permissions to the current context. This is not yet the execution of dangerous operations, but only a check that they are allowed.
  4. Controlled action beyond the original trust boundary. The researcher performs the minimum safe action that confirms the previously obtained permissions work in practice. For example, they create a test record in a neighboring tenant (usually a second test tenant).

The first two stages only produce a hypothesis that the trust boundary has been violated. The object is visible on the network and accepts requests, but that does not mean the researcher can change anything in it. Confirmed impact appears only in the last two stages, when the researcher obtains authorization and performs a controlled action beyond the original boundary. For example, network reachability of a neighboring database indicates insufficient network isolation, but cross-tenant impact appears only when the researcher can use the original context to perform an action on another tenant’s resource that the cloud model doesn’t allow, such as reading data. To keep the test ethical, the researcher demonstrates such reading only between their own test accounts, so real users’ data stays confidential.

Attacker model and three research goals

Dividing the cloud infrastructure into three layers (External, Overlay, and Underlay) helps define the attacker model for each layer. In penetration testing, the researcher can focus on one layer and look for every possible way to violate the nearest trust boundary. Another approach is to build a full attack chain across all layers. The attacker model also defines the starting point: the access level and position from which the pentest begins. Below is a general list of attacker models that apply to most cloud infrastructures:

  1. External attacker without an account. The test covers the public attack surface, registration, the login mechanism, externally accessible services, and the path to the first tenant context. Layer: External.
  2. Attacker with legitimate tenant access. This is the key model for a multi-tenant cloud: the tenant is entitled to create their own resources and tries to go beyond the limits those resources impose. Layer: External.
  3. Internal attacker with a compromised runtime. The starting point is a compromised process, pod, or virtual machine. This scenario is especially relevant for supply chain attacks. The researcher explores options for lateral movement in the network and host environment. Layer: Overlay or Underlay.
  4. Internal attacker with a compromised IAM service account token or an operator account. This model involves testing IAM and the cloud platform management processes. Layer: Overlay or Underlay.

Regardless of the attacker model and the initial entry point, the research goals at the initial stage fall into three groups.

1. Code execution first

The goal of this approach is to execute arbitrary code inside a provider-managed environment. To do this, a pentester can attack a managed database, serverless function, CI/CD workload, PaaS application, tenant virtual machine, container, or virtual network gateway.

Example of an attack chain through a managed service

The pentester interacts with the managed service interface and finds a vulnerability in it (for example, CVE-2026-19478 in the case of the GitLab web interface) or in add-on modules deployed by the cloud provider. The vulnerability allows the researcher to execute code remotely inside the runtime (operating system), find an IAM service account, and use it to gain access to the resource management service. The researcher can then look for vulnerabilities in that service and penetrate the provider overlay.



Example of an attack chain through a virtual environment

The chain begins with the compromise of a tenant workload. The researcher plants malicious code in a popular OS or container image in advance. A cloud tenant downloads and runs the trojanized image, and the attacker gains access inside that specific container. Next, the attacker finds ways to escape the container (using CVE-2026-43284) into the runtime: the container runtime, hypervisor, or host agent. From there, they reach the host shared with other containers and can affect the provider’s management components.

2. Credentials first

Rather than gaining access to a runtime environment, the researcher may obtain credentials that cloud services accept as valid: a service account token, metadata access credentials, an mTLS certificate, a bootstrap token, or an object storage key.

In this scenario, the move into the provider overlay doesn’t come from breaking network isolation. It happens through legitimate platform functionality. The network may be well segmented, but an over-privileged IAM service account token that the attacker manages to extract (for example, from environment variables or metadata) can legitimately call an internal API through a standard gateway or token exchange service.

3. Administrative or service context

The goal of this scenario is to bypass technical restrictions by gaining legitimate access through channels intended for staff. The route often starts with targeting people (phishing, insiders, or leaked employee or contractor credentials). However, the final entry point into the internal environment is technical: a connection through the operator’s VPN, a support portal, a remote support tool, an administrative workstation, an SSH certificate, or a serial console. Although the route often starts with compromising a person, the resulting initial zone (the technical context with certain privileges and access to resources where the researcher ends up) can match the first scenario. For example, access to a managed database host (DBaaS host) can be obtained not by exploiting a vulnerability but through a legitimate administrative channel, which is then used for privilege escalation.

Sorting out the architectural zoo

After moving deeper into the cloud infrastructure and gaining access to a node, the pentester analyzes local artifacts. Completely different architectures can hide behind the same managed service.

OpenStack-like infrastructure

IaaS services based on OpenStack usually include a large set of components: an IAM service account, compute resources, networking, images and block storage, as well as API processes, workers, a message broker, and platform state databases. A managed service built on top of such an IaaS layer can use a separate virtual machine for each database instance, several instances on a shared virtual machine, a Kubernetes cluster on virtual workers, or even a dedicated tenant for a specific product.

A message broker such as RabbitMQ is typical for OpenStack, but finding one doesn’t prove that the target is a stock OpenStack deployment. The provider may have changed the trust model, added its own API, and replaced some of the components.

Kubernetes-based platforms

In clouds of this type, a central Kubernetes cluster controls the entire infrastructure: not only containers but also virtual machines, other tenant Kubernetes clusters, and managed services. At the service runtime level, a product can run as a pod in a shared namespace, an application inside a tenant, a KubeVirt virtual machine, or a worker node of a separate cluster. From the outside, they all look like the same product, but their trust boundaries and the attack surface behind them differ radically.

Because the platform is managed through a Kubernetes cluster, where the service account token is the main unit of authorization, it’s especially important to determine where the IAM service account you obtained during the pentest lives: in a tenant cluster, in a managed cluster, or with an operator that serves multiple tenants. Identical-looking tokens may have permissions for only one pod, or they may allow changing resources in several environments at once.

Custom control plane and configuration management systems

A provider may forgo off-the-shelf platforms altogether. For example, in this kind of architecture, a provider might build its public API in-house, deploy virtual machines through libvirt or a lightweight IaaS layer, automate networking with scripts around Open vSwitch (OVS), build object storage on Ceph, and distribute node configuration through SaltStack or another configuration management system.

In this architecture, a virtual machine management service might get its settings from an internal HTTP service, a script with shared credentials might run backups, billing might receive events from a queue, and an internal agent might talk to the control plane over mTLS. Almost every component here is specific to the provider. The main risk area is not vulnerabilities in well-known products, such as those built on open-source solutions, but logic errors at the junctions between internal systems.

Mixed-stack platform

In practice, the most common setup is a mix of approaches

  1. The infrastructure core (IaaS layer) is built on OpenStack
  2. Kubernetes runs the managed services
  3. The storage system runs on Ceph
  4. IAM, billing systems, and the internal API are custom-built.

Here are some clues that can help form initial hypotheses about the environment:

  • A Kubernetes token and cluster DNS in the runtime environment of the host under investigation suggest that the service is running in the context of a pod.
  • A running qemu-guest-agent process indicates that we are inside a virtual machine rather than on a physical server.
  • Attached Ceph/RBD volumes point to a separate storage plane in the platform architecture, implemented as distributed block storage.
  • A large number of CNI or Open vSwitch (OVS) network interfaces means that this is a shared Kubernetes node

However, any such clue needs additional verification tests.

Example of a mixed-stack cloud platform

How to choose the next trust boundary

After the pentester has examined the initial zone, the next route depends on a combination of two factors:

  1. Network visibility: which segments, services, and tenants are reachable.
  2. Available trust level: which credentials, certificates, and API methods are accepted as valid in those segments.

Sometimes the network has almost no restrictions, but all services require correct mTLS authentication. In other cases, the network is almost completely closed, but a discovered service account can create resources across the entire region through the standard API. For this reason, network reachability (open ports) and the IAM service account must be considered together.

At this stage, the researcher usually focuses on several critical areas:

Telemetry (observability): the pentester checks whether centralized monitoring systems (logs, metrics, traces) collect data from different tenants and whether there is sufficient isolation between them. Isolation can fail if an attacker can search by other tenants’ identifiers, read raw event records, extract credentials from telemetry events, or influence alerts and automated actions.

item.title: Ransomware at the hypervisor layer: how attackers use ESXi and vCenter features for malicious purposes
item.description:
Authors

  • Elsayed Elrefaei
  • Mohamed Ghobashy

Our Global Emergency Response Team (GERT) recently investigated an engagement in which an adversary destroyed an organization’s virtualization estate over a 10-day period. The campaign targeted four ESXi hosts, every virtual machine hosted on them, both vCenter Server Appliances, and all connected backup infrastructure. The ransom notes identified the attacker as the BlackNevas group, first observed in November 2024. What’s interesting about this attack is that no virtualization layer vulnerabilities were exploited: no guest-to-host escapes, no hypervisor memory corruption. Every action taken against ESXi was executed through legitimate VMware management interfaces.

In September 2021, the Babuk ransomware source code was leaked online, including its ESXi version, which made ESXi ransomware accessible to cybercriminals with relatively low technical skills. At least ten subsequent ransomware families have leveraged this leaked code, including groups that otherwise lacked the expertise to develop ESXi-compatible ransomware lockers from scratch. We saw multiple operators using Babuk-derived ESXi lockers along with the leaked LockBit Windows builds. It is worth noting that while the Babuk ESXi version may target both old and up-to-date systems, the target organizations run unsupported ESXi versions, making them easier to attack.

This article examines why the hypervisor layer remains difficult to monitor, what common access paths adversaries use to reach it, and how they establish persistence on the management plane. We’ll also look into the architecture of ESXi encryptors, the deliberate destruction of backup infrastructure, and the log sources that enable post-incident reconstruction. At the end of this article, we’ll provide indicators of compromise recovered during the investigation.

Ten days of dwell time from initial access to the destructive phase. Timeline reconstructed from incident evidence

Why the hypervisor changes ransomware economics

Virtualization enables cost-effective and efficient resource management, simplifies simultaneous updates and policy enforcement. However, at the same time it reduces the number of control points and enables broader impact in case of a cyberattack. In non-virtualized environments, a single guest compromise normally affects one operating system. Compromise of the virtualization management plane gives the attacker access to many hypervisor hosts, while direct impact on an ESXi datastore can render many guest systems unavailable at once. This makes the hypervisor layer an attractive target for ransomware operators, especially when domain controllers, application servers, databases, and backup workloads share the same virtualized estate.

According to Kaspersky’s global cybersecurity services report, ransomware accounted for 39.4% of incidents GERT handled in 2025, and the data for the beginning of 2026 shows that it remains a major threat. Back in 2023, SentinelOne documented that multiple ransomware families are using ESXi lockers derived from the leaked Babuk source code, which lowered the development barrier for actors who otherwise lacked the necessary expertise to build ESXi-capable samples. This makes ransomware targeting virtualization environments more accessible to a broader range of threat actors, and this trend is still with us.

The visibility asymmetry

ESXi is a specialized hypervisor based on VMware’s proprietary VMkernel. It shares certain similarities with Linux (and other Unix-like systems), accepts Linux commands and runs certain Linux-like software, but it is different from general-purpose Linux distributions. Broadcom states that off-the-shelf security tools designed for general-purpose operating systems cannot run on ESXi without workarounds and that direct installation of third-party agents or antiviruses on ESXi and vCenter Server Appliance (VCSA) is not supported. Defenders therefore rely heavily on built-in hardening, management-plane telemetry, agentless security solution integrations, and telemetry collection from the infrastructure outside ESXi hosts.

Guest operating systems are usually protected by EDR software, but if an ESXi-side process modifies a virtual machine disk (VMDK) or related datastore file, an EDR agent inside a guest cannot directly observe or attribute the hypervisor process performing the operation. Guest telemetry may record consequences, such as I/O failures or an abrupt shutdown, but the malicious execution occurs outside its boundary. In the engagement examined here, this made host-native and management-plane telemetry central to the incident timeline reconstruction.

How attackers reach the virtualization layer

There are different routes into the environment that require different controls, but can ultimately provide access to the centralized virtualization management plane and the ESXi hosts it controls. In this article, we’ll look into four main routes that may lead to virtualization infrastructure compromise:

  • Vulnerability exploitation
  • Credential reuse from the Windows estate
  • Active Directory integration abuse
  • Backup infrastructure as a credential bridge

The virtualization trust stack and recurring entry paths

Vulnerability exploitation

In the incident we analyzed, there was no evidence pointing to an ESXi vulnerability as the initial access path. Nevertheless, public vulnerabilities remain important because they have been used to compromise the virtualization management infrastructure. With the exploits available online, this is one of the most probable entry routes. Below you can find several examples of vulnerabilities affecting virtualization environments that have been seen exploited by the attackers. For example, the Twelve group chained CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2021-22005 to plant a web shell directly on a vCenter appliance, which loaded a backdoor that then established persistence by injecting a shared object into the SSH daemon. Note that these vulnerabilities are not related to the incident in question and they are provided merely as an initial access vector illustration, which could help defenders define their relevant attack surface and prioritize patching activities.

CVE Layer Security effect KEV* Why it matters here
CVE-2021-21974 ESXi OpenSLP Remote code execution in vulnerable OpenSLP service No Historically associated with discussion around the ESXiArgs ransomware.
CVE-2021-22005 vCenter Server Arbitrary file upload leading to remote code execution Yes Documented use in ransomware-related activity.
CVE-2021-21972 vCenter plugin Unauthenticated RCE via vSphere Client plugin Yes Documented use in ransomware-related activity.
CVE-2021-21985 vCenter VSAN Health Check plugin Remote code execution Yes Documented use in ransomware-related activity.
CVE-2023-34048 vCenter DCERPC Out-of-bounds write leading to RCE Yes Known exploited vulnerability affecting vCenter. Although there’s no data about its involvement in ransomware incidents, it is worth noting due to its impact on the virtualization management plane.
CVE-2024-37085 ESXi AD integration AD permissions can become full ESXi administration Yes Documented use in ransomware-related activity. It also highlights the risks arising from the relationship between AD identities and administrative access to ESXi.
CVE-2024-38812 / 38813 vCenter DCERPC RCE / privilege escalation to root Yes Known exploited vulnerabilities affecting vCenter. Although there’s no data about their involvement in ransomware incidents, they are worth noting due to their impact on the virtualization management plane.
CVE-2025-22224 / 22225 / 22226 ESXi / Workstation / Fusion Guest-to-host chain requiring prior guest privileges Yes Known exploited vulnerabilities allowing attackers to perform a guest-to-host attack chain. CVE-2025-22225 exploitation has been seen in ransomware incidents. However, this attack chain requires privileged access to a guest VM, which makes it less critical than unauthenticated RCEs.

* Known Exploited Vulnerabilities database maintained by CISA. KEV status indicates that exploitation of a vulnerability has been observed in the wild, but does not by itself indicate ransomware use. Where ransomware use is documented, it is stated separately. Neither KEV status nor known exploitation by ransomware actors means that the vulnerability was used in the incident in question.

Active Directory integration

CVE-2024-37085 is a useful illustration of why it is crucial to authenticate to different systems separately even when the hypervisor itself is patched. The vulnerability affects ESXi hosts configured to use AD for user management. According to Microsoft, it is exploited by ransomware operators, including Akira and Black Basta, abusing the ESX Admins group behavior to obtain full ESXi administration. CISA lists the issue in their KEV catalog and notes that it has been used in ransomware incidents.

The vulnerability is fixed in ESXi 8.0 U3. For older systems, Broadcom recommends the following workaround:

  • Change the esxAdminsGroupAutoAdd value from true to false.
  • Change authValidateInterval from 1440 to 90 minutes.
  • Clear the default ESX Admins group mapping where appropriate.

These controls reduce exposure, but the architectural lesson is broader: domain compromise should not automatically allow the adversary to obtain hypervisor admin rights.

Recommendation for defenders

Avoid unnecessary direct Active Directory dependency on ESXi hosts. Where business requirements demand it, stick to the principle of least privilege: add only those accounts to administrative groups that really need this level of access, use separate admin accounts with separate credentials for the domain and for hypervisors, restrict access to the ESXi and vCenter management interfaces to only those network segments, accounts and workstations that are necessary to control it, and continuously validate ESXi permission changes. vCenter role-based access control (RBAC) and identity federation should be configured for virtualization administration, while ordinary enterprise credentials and broad domain groups should not be used to access vCenter or ESXi with high privileges.

Credential reuse from the Windows estate

The third path requires no vulnerability. Administrative credentials present on domain controllers, jump servers, backup systems, identity infrastructure or administrator workstations may provide access to vCenter or ESXi if the same admin accounts are used across different infrastructure segments. MITRE ATT&CK treats the Valid Accounts technique as applicable to ESXi and specifically notes that compromised default or domain accounts can provide privileged access to other systems.

In this incident , credentials obtained from non-virtualization systems inside the organization’s perimeter were used to reach the vCenter Server Appliances. Unlike vulnerability exploitation, successful authentication with a valid account may appear operationally normal. To reliably detect such activity, analysts must therefore evaluate the source host, account history, time, destination, subsequent administrative actions, and whether the authenticated account normally manages virtualization infrastructure.

Backup infrastructure as a credential bridge

Backup platforms are not passive storage. They commonly require service accounts, hypervisor credentials, repository access and broad network reach so they can protect and restore critical workloads. This makes the backup server a concentrated trust point. In this incident, the adversary extracted stored credentials after gaining administrative execution on backup infrastructure, creating a route toward other infrastructure tiers.

Persistence on the management plane

With the potential risk possibilities explained, let’s go back to our case study. The attackers managed to compromise via SSH the vCenter appliance managing virtualization disaster recovery where they established two layers of persistence. The first used MeshAgent, the endpoint component of the legitimate MeshCentral remote management platform. The second used Ligolo-ng as a reverse tunnel implemented as a systemd service. This activity maps to two ATT&CK techniques: Systemd Service (T1543.002) and Protocol Tunneling (T1572).

The timeline was as follows. The attackers authenticated on the appliance as root via SSH. Forty-three seconds later, they fetched and deployed MeshAgent through a shell script. The SSH session lasted 2 minutes and 26 seconds in total. After it ended, the adversary didn’t use SSH to access the compromised appliance anymore, thus reducing the usefulness of monitoring focused only on interactive SSH sessions. Roughly four hours later, they returned through MeshAgent and installed the Ligolo-ng tunnel as a persistent systemd unit.

The unit uses a VMware-like prefix, places its binary under /opt/vmware/bin/, describes plausible appliance housekeeping functions, and requests Restart=always. A defender should not treat any unrecognized VMware-looking service as malicious by default, because custom integrations may exist, but a service absent from the list of services the organization defines as trusted is a high-confidence anomaly requiring immediate validation.

Beyond the incident in question, more advanced ESXi persistence techniques have also been documented. For example, Mandiant observed attackers using malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) as a persistence mechanism on compromised ESXi hosts. This demonstrates that attackers with administrative access can establish persistent access at the hypervisor layer, including persistence that survives host restarts. However, this incident shows that common remote-management software and a systemd service can be sufficient when vCenter itself is trusted and poorly monitored.

Turning vCenter into an offensive control plane

One interesting technique observed in the incident was the use of vCenter Host Profiles. Host Profiles are intended to capture and enforce configuration across ESXi hosts. A Host Profile can be applied to separate hosts, clusters of hosts or all hosts associated with a profile. It also may contain subprofiles covering specific configuration aspects, e.g., authentication. Among other things, Host Profiles may contain configuration for Tech Support Mode (TSM) and TSM-SSH.

In this incident, the adversary used Host Profiles to change TSM-SSH service state to enable SSH on target ESXi hosts. The evidence recorded the following sequence:

Offset Source Observed event Primary evidence
T+0 vCenter Host configuration read through Host Profile workflow vpxa.log
T+10m18s vCenter Configuration change pushed to enable SSH vpxa.log
T+10m51s vCenter / ESXi TSM-SSH service reached RUNNING state, indicating that SSH has been enabled on the host and it is accessible from a remote device vpxa.log + vobd.log

Host Profile manipulation sequence observed before direct ESXi access

Note that the 33-second interval between the configuration push and TSM-SSH reaching RUNNING state is short enough for us to be able to quickly correlate these events by comparing logs from different sources. Overall, it took the attacker eleven minutes after the initial configuration read to reconfigure the host from policy-disabled SSH to direct remote access support. Subsequently, direct SSH access to the target ESXi hosts originated from the vCenter appliance IP, a source that would normally be considered highly trusted on the management network.

Compromise of the management plane converted a legitimate compliance mechanism into an access path to the managed hypervisor

Why ESXi configuration change via vCenter is a trust-boundary failure

Host hardening is important, but centrally administered controls should not be considered independent once the central management tool is compromised. If vCenter has authority to modify host state, an attacker controlling it may be able to make a malicious change look structurally similar to legitimate compliance activity: read configuration, apply a desired state, and observe the result. The distinguishing context becomes authorization, the timing, the source account, the change window, and whether the desired state itself weakens security.

This is why vCenter should be treated as a Tier 0 asset and provided with the highest possible level of protection. Management-plane administrative accounts should be isolated from ordinary enterprise administration, network access should be restricted to dedicated management paths, high-risk configuration changes should require strong authentication and monitoring, and vCenter-to-ESXi traffic should be thoroughly compared to a normal behavior baseline (connection patterns, ports, protocols, source and destination systems) rather than implicitly trusted. All significant discrepancies should be treated as suspicious and investigated.

High-fidelity detection opportunity

An alert should be generated when Host Profile compliance (or remediation in VMware terms) changes TSM or TSM-SSH configuration outside an approved window, particularly when followed by a new SSH session from vCenter or another management appliance. This sequence is more precise than alerting on SSH alone because each step is legitimate in isolation but dangerous in combination.

Notes on ESXi abuse: living-off-the-land tools and controls to monitor

Once an attacker can administer ESXi, many destructive actions require no exploit. LOLESXi project catalogs native ESXi binaries and scripts that have been abused by threat actors, including administrative utilities that enumerate VMs, control power state and alter configuration. This mirrors living-off-the-land behavior on Windows, but the target is the hypervisor control plane.

There are two ESXi hardening mechanisms, and changes to either can be viewed as highly suspicious. Host acceptance level controls which VIBs are allowed to install. The execInstalledOnly setting controls whether non-installed binaries may execute. Broadcom states that ESXi 8 enables the execInstalledOnly runtime option by default and warns that disabling it allows unknown non-installed binaries to execute, increasing ransomware risk. There is also a kernel enforcement setting with the same name, which is related to the runtime option, but distinct. Changes to that may require a reboot.

Control What it governs Why a change is suspicious Useful evidence
Host acceptance level Which VIB packages can be installed Lowering to a less trusted level expands what the host will accept esxcli / config events / esxupdate.log
execInstalledOnly runtime Execution of binaries not installed through VIB packages Value 0/FALSE permits non-installed code to run vobd.log + advanced settings
execInstalledOnly kernel enforcement Stronger VMkernel boot-level enforcement that restricts execution to files that were installed through VIB packages and were not subsequently modified. Weakening may require a reboot and changes the security baseline kernel settings + boot history

ESXi controls that the attackers may try to weaken

Inside the ESXi impact phase

Stopping virtual machines before impact

Mature ESXi lockers generally stop guest machines before modifying virtual-disk data because running VMs hold active state and file locks. Different families implement this in different ways, which creates useful behavioral detections. The families described below are not related to the incident in question, but these descriptions may be useful for ransomware protection in general.

Authors

  • Elsayed Elrefaei
  • Mohamed Ghobashy

Our Global Emergency Response Team (GERT) recently investigated an engagement in which an adversary destroyed an organization’s virtualization estate over a 10-day period. The campaign targeted four ESXi hosts, every virtual machine hosted on them, both vCenter Server Appliances, and all connected backup infrastructure. The ransom notes identified the attacker as the BlackNevas group, first observed in November 2024. What’s interesting about this attack is that no virtualization layer vulnerabilities were exploited: no guest-to-host escapes, no hypervisor memory corruption. Every action taken against ESXi was executed through legitimate VMware management interfaces.

In September 2021, the Babuk ransomware source code was leaked online, including its ESXi version, which made ESXi ransomware accessible to cybercriminals with relatively low technical skills. At least ten subsequent ransomware families have leveraged this leaked code, including groups that otherwise lacked the expertise to develop ESXi-compatible ransomware lockers from scratch. We saw multiple operators using Babuk-derived ESXi lockers along with the leaked LockBit Windows builds. It is worth noting that while the Babuk ESXi version may target both old and up-to-date systems, the target organizations run unsupported ESXi versions, making them easier to attack.

This article examines why the hypervisor layer remains difficult to monitor, what common access paths adversaries use to reach it, and how they establish persistence on the management plane. We’ll also look into the architecture of ESXi encryptors, the deliberate destruction of backup infrastructure, and the log sources that enable post-incident reconstruction. At the end of this article, we’ll provide indicators of compromise recovered during the investigation.

Ten days of dwell time from initial access to the destructive phase. Timeline reconstructed from incident evidence

Why the hypervisor changes ransomware economics

Virtualization enables cost-effective and efficient resource management, simplifies simultaneous updates and policy enforcement. However, at the same time it reduces the number of control points and enables broader impact in case of a cyberattack. In non-virtualized environments, a single guest compromise normally affects one operating system. Compromise of the virtualization management plane gives the attacker access to many hypervisor hosts, while direct impact on an ESXi datastore can render many guest systems unavailable at once. This makes the hypervisor layer an attractive target for ransomware operators, especially when domain controllers, application servers, databases, and backup workloads share the same virtualized estate.

According to Kaspersky’s global cybersecurity services report, ransomware accounted for 39.4% of incidents GERT handled in 2025, and the data for the beginning of 2026 shows that it remains a major threat. Back in 2023, SentinelOne documented that multiple ransomware families are using ESXi lockers derived from the leaked Babuk source code, which lowered the development barrier for actors who otherwise lacked the necessary expertise to build ESXi-capable samples. This makes ransomware targeting virtualization environments more accessible to a broader range of threat actors, and this trend is still with us.

The visibility asymmetry

ESXi is a specialized hypervisor based on VMware’s proprietary VMkernel. It shares certain similarities with Linux (and other Unix-like systems), accepts Linux commands and runs certain Linux-like software, but it is different from general-purpose Linux distributions. Broadcom states that off-the-shelf security tools designed for general-purpose operating systems cannot run on ESXi without workarounds and that direct installation of third-party agents or antiviruses on ESXi and vCenter Server Appliance (VCSA) is not supported. Defenders therefore rely heavily on built-in hardening, management-plane telemetry, agentless security solution integrations, and telemetry collection from the infrastructure outside ESXi hosts.

Guest operating systems are usually protected by EDR software, but if an ESXi-side process modifies a virtual machine disk (VMDK) or related datastore file, an EDR agent inside a guest cannot directly observe or attribute the hypervisor process performing the operation. Guest telemetry may record consequences, such as I/O failures or an abrupt shutdown, but the malicious execution occurs outside its boundary. In the engagement examined here, this made host-native and management-plane telemetry central to the incident timeline reconstruction.

How attackers reach the virtualization layer

There are different routes into the environment that require different controls, but can ultimately provide access to the centralized virtualization management plane and the ESXi hosts it controls. In this article, we’ll look into four main routes that may lead to virtualization infrastructure compromise:

  • Vulnerability exploitation
  • Credential reuse from the Windows estate
  • Active Directory integration abuse
  • Backup infrastructure as a credential bridge

The virtualization trust stack and recurring entry paths

Vulnerability exploitation

In the incident we analyzed, there was no evidence pointing to an ESXi vulnerability as the initial access path. Nevertheless, public vulnerabilities remain important because they have been used to compromise the virtualization management infrastructure. With the exploits available online, this is one of the most probable entry routes. Below you can find several examples of vulnerabilities affecting virtualization environments that have been seen exploited by the attackers. For example, the Twelve group chained CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2021-22005 to plant a web shell directly on a vCenter appliance, which loaded a backdoor that then established persistence by injecting a shared object into the SSH daemon. Note that these vulnerabilities are not related to the incident in question and they are provided merely as an initial access vector illustration, which could help defenders define their relevant attack surface and prioritize patching activities.

CVE-2021-21974 ESXi OpenSLP Remote code execution in vulnerable OpenSLP service No Historically associated with discussion around the ESXiArgs ransomware.
CVE-2021-22005 vCenter Server Arbitrary file upload leading to remote code execution Yes Documented use in ransomware-related activity.
CVE-2021-21972 vCenter plugin Unauthenticated RCE via vSphere Client plugin Yes Documented use in ransomware-related activity.

Where ransomware use is documented, it is stated separately. Neither KEV status nor known exploitation by ransomware actors means that the vulnerability was used in the incident in question.

Active Directory integration

CVE-2024-37085 is a useful illustration of why it is crucial to authenticate to different systems separately even when the hypervisor itself is patched. The vulnerability affects ESXi hosts configured to use AD for user management. According to Microsoft, it is exploited by ransomware operators, including Akira and Black Basta, abusing the ESX Admins group behavior to obtain full ESXi administration. CISA lists the issue in their KEV catalog and notes that it has been used in ransomware incidents.

The vulnerability is fixed in ESXi 8.0 U3. For older systems, Broadcom recommends the following workaround:

  • Change the esxAdminsGroupAutoAdd value from true to false.
  • Change authValidateInterval from 1440 to 90 minutes.
  • Clear the default ESX Admins group mapping where appropriate.

These controls reduce exposure, but the architectural lesson is broader: domain compromise should not automatically allow the adversary to obtain hypervisor admin rights.

Recommendation for defenders

Avoid unnecessary direct Active Directory dependency on ESXi hosts. Where business requirements demand it, stick to the principle of least privilege: add only those accounts to administrative groups that really need this level of access, use separate admin accounts with separate credentials for the domain and for hypervisors, restrict access to the ESXi and vCenter management interfaces to only those network segments, accounts and workstations that are necessary to control it, and continuously validate ESXi permission changes. vCenter role-based access control (RBAC) and identity federation should be configured for virtualization administration, while ordinary enterprise credentials and broad domain groups should not be used to access vCenter or ESXi with high privileges.

Credential reuse from the Windows estate

The third path requires no vulnerability. Administrative credentials present on domain controllers, jump servers, backup systems, identity infrastructure or administrator workstations may provide access to vCenter or ESXi if the same admin accounts are used across different infrastructure segments. MITRE ATT&CK treats the Valid Accounts technique as applicable to ESXi and specifically notes that compromised default or domain accounts can provide privileged access to other systems.

In this incident , credentials obtained from non-virtualization systems inside the organization’s perimeter were used to reach the vCenter Server Appliances. Unlike vulnerability exploitation, successful authentication with a valid account may appear operationally normal. To reliably detect such activity, analysts must therefore evaluate the source host, account history, time, destination, subsequent administrative actions, and whether the authenticated account normally manages virtualization infrastructure.

Backup infrastructure as a credential bridge

Backup platforms are not passive storage. They commonly require service accounts, hypervisor credentials, repository access and broad network reach so they can protect and restore critical workloads. This makes the backup server a concentrated trust point. In this incident, the adversary extracted stored credentials after gaining administrative execution on backup infrastructure, creating a route toward other infrastructure tiers.

Persistence on the management plane

With the potential risk possibilities explained, let’s go back to our case study. The attackers managed to compromise via SSH the vCenter appliance managing virtualization disaster recovery where they established two layers of persistence. The first used MeshAgent, the endpoint component of the legitimate MeshCentral remote management platform. The second used Ligolo-ng as a reverse tunnel implemented as a systemd service. This activity maps to two ATT&CK techniques: Systemd Service (T1543.002) and Protocol Tunneling (T1572).

The timeline was as follows. The attackers authenticated on the appliance as root via SSH. Forty-three seconds later, they fetched and deployed MeshAgent through a shell script. The SSH session lasted 2 minutes and 26 seconds in total. After it ended, the adversary didn’t use SSH to access the compromised appliance anymore, thus reducing the usefulness of monitoring focused only on interactive SSH sessions. Roughly four hours later, they returned through MeshAgent and installed the Ligolo-ng tunnel as a persistent systemd unit.

One interesting technique observed in the incident was the use of vCenter Host Profiles. Host Profiles are intended to capture and enforce configuration across ESXi hosts. A Host Profile can be applied to separate hosts, clusters of hosts or all hosts associated with a profile. It also may contain subprofiles covering specific configuration aspects, e.g., authentication. Among other things, Host Profiles may contain configuration for Tech Support Mode (TSM) and TSM-SSH.

Offset Source Observed event Primary evidence
T+0 vCenter Host configuration read through Host Profile workflow vpxa.log
T+10m18s vCenter Configuration change pushed to enable SSH vpxa.log
T+10m51s vCenter / ESXi TSM-SSH service reached RUNNING state, indicating that SSH has been enabled on the host and it is accessible from a remote device vpxa.log + vobd.log

Overall, it took the attacker eleven minutes after the initial configuration read to reconfigure the host from policy-disabled SSH to direct remote access support. Subsequently, direct SSH access to the target ESXi hosts originated from the vCenter appliance IP, a source that would normally be considered highly trusted on the management network.

Compromise of the management plane converted a legitimate compliance mechanism into an access path to the managed hypervisor

Why ESXi configuration change via vCenter is a trust-boundary failure

Host hardening is important, but centrally administered controls should not be considered independent once the central management tool is compromised. If vCenter has authority to modify host state, an attacker controlling it may be able to make a malicious change look structurally similar to legitimate compliance activity: read configuration, apply a desired state, and observe the result. The distinguishing context becomes authorization, the timing, the source account, the change window, and whether the desired state itself weakens security.

This is why vCenter should be treated as a Tier 0 asset and provided with the highest possible level of protection. Management-plane administrative accounts should be isolated from ordinary enterprise administration, network access should be restricted to dedicated management paths, high-risk configuration changes should require strong authentication and monitoring, and vCenter-to-ESXi traffic should be thoroughly compared to a normal behavior baseline (connection patterns, ports, protocols, source and destination systems) rather than implicitly trusted. All significant discrepancies should be treated as suspicious and investigated.

High-fidelity detection opportunity

An alert should be generated when Host Profile compliance (or remediation in VMware terms) changes TSM or TSM-SSH configuration outside an approved window, particularly when followed by a new SSH session from vCenter or another management appliance. This sequence is more precise than alerting on SSH alone because each step is legitimate in isolation but dangerous in combination.

Once an attacker can administer ESXi, many destructive actions require no exploit. LOLESXi project catalogs native ESXi binaries and scripts that have been abused by threat actors, including administrative utilities that enumerate VMs, control power state and alter configuration.
